facts.fact: When a phone takes a photo with location services on, it can write the exact GPS coordinates of where the photo was taken into hidden data in the file, called EXIF metadata.
facts.hook: a student checks the details of a photo a friend sent and sees a map pin on the friend's own street

facts.fact: Big social networks such as Facebook and Instagram remove GPS data from the photos other people see, but a photo sent as an email attachment usually keeps its location data.
facts.hook: a kid emails vacation photos to a club list and a sibling points out what the files still carry

facts.fact: Deleting a post removes it from your page, but anyone who already took a screenshot or saved a copy still has it.
facts.hook: an embarrassing post is deleted after ten minutes, then turns up in a group chat the next day

facts.fact: Since 1996 the Internet Archive has been saving copies of public web pages, and its Wayback Machine lets anyone look at old versions of many websites.
facts.hook: a student finds their old, forgotten blog still readable in an online archive

facts.fact: In the United States, a 1998 law called COPPA says websites and apps must get a parent's permission before collecting personal information from children under 13.
facts.hook: a sign-up screen asks for a birth date, and a sixth grader wonders why the age matters

facts.fact: Snapchat's Snap Map, launched in 2017, can show a user's real-time location to their friends on a map.
facts.hook: a friend knows exactly which store someone is in at the mall without being told

facts.fact: Snapchat has a setting called Ghost Mode that hides your location on Snap Map, so no one else, not even your friends, can see where you are.
facts.hook: a student at the dinner table realizes their map pin has been showing their house all week

facts.fact: Details in the background of a photo, such as a street sign, a house number or a school logo, can let a stranger work out where it was taken.
facts.hook: before posting a selfie from the front porch, a kid zooms in and spots the house number

facts.fact: Setting an account to private limits who can see your posts, but anyone you have already accepted as a follower can still copy or share what they see.
facts.hook: a private post gets forwarded by a follower the owner barely knew

facts.fact: Search engines use automated programs called crawlers to copy and index public web pages, so something posted publicly can turn up in search results.
facts.hook: a student searches their own name and finds a public comment they wrote years ago

facts.fact: In the European Union, a law called the GDPR, in force since May 2018, gives people a right to ask companies to erase their personal data in certain circumstances.
facts.hook: a family that moved from Europe asks an app to delete an old account and gets an answer

facts.fact: iPhones and Android phones let you choose, app by app, whether an app may use your location always, only while you are using it, or never.
facts.hook: a kid at a school computer lab helps a friend find which game has been tracking location all the time

facts.fact: Printers mix colors from four inks, cyan, magenta, yellow and black, which is why it is called CMYK; the K stands for 'key', the plate that printed black.
facts.hook: a poster prints with strange colors and the librarian explains the four ink cartridges

facts.fact: In his book Opticks, first published in 1704, Isaac Newton arranged the colors of the spectrum in a circle, an early form of the color wheel.
facts.hook: a student designing a color wheel for an art project wonders who drew the first one

facts.fact: On drawing pencils, H is usually read as 'hardness' and B as 'blackness', so a 6B pencil makes darker, softer marks than a 4H.
facts.hook: a sketch comes out too faint because the artist grabbed the wrong pencil from the box

facts.fact: Most pencil cores are graphite powder mixed with clay, and adding more clay makes a harder pencil that leaves lighter marks.
facts.hook: a kid at a grandparent's table wonders why two pencils of the same size draw so differently

facts.fact: Pencil 'lead' has never contained the metal lead; the name comes from early writers mistaking graphite for a kind of lead ore.
facts.hook: a younger cousin is afraid of being poisoned by a pencil and needs reassuring

facts.fact: The Japanese word origami comes from 'ori', meaning to fold, and 'kami', meaning paper.
facts.hook: a library origami club argues over what the word actually means

facts.fact: Complementary colors sit opposite each other on the color wheel, such as red and green, and mixing two complementary paints produces a dull brown or gray.
facts.hook: a painter keeps turning a sunset muddy and cannot figure out why

facts.fact: Acrylic paint is thinned with water while wet, but once it dries it becomes water-resistant, so brushes must be washed before the paint dries on them.
facts.hook: a set of brushes left overnight at the studio has turned stiff as sticks

facts.fact: Oil paint does not dry by water evaporating; its oil slowly reacts with oxygen in the air, so an oil painting can take days or longer to dry to the touch.
facts.hook: a student plans to carry a fresh oil painting home the same afternoon

facts.fact: Clay pieces must be completely dry before they are fired in a kiln, because leftover water turns to steam and can crack or burst the piece.
facts.hook: a studio teacher sets aside a student's still-damp bowl instead of loading it into the kiln

facts.fact: The rule of thirds is a composition guideline that divides a picture into a three-by-three grid and places the main subject along those lines or where they cross.
facts.hook: a drawing feels boring until the subject is moved away from the exact center

facts.fact: Scoring a line on thick card with a blunt tool before folding it gives a straight, clean fold instead of a cracked, bumpy one.
facts.hook: a homemade greeting card keeps cracking along the fold

facts.fact: After flying across time zones, the body clock adjusts at an average of about one day for each hour of time difference.
facts.hook: a family that flew six hours of time zones is still wide awake at midnight on day two

facts.fact: Most travelers find jet lag harder to adjust to after flying east than after flying west.
facts.hook: a kid who felt fine after the trip out feels awful after the flight home

facts.fact: Airliner cabins are pressurized, but under regulations the cabin air pressure may be as low as it would be at 8,000 feet (about 2,400 meters) above sea level.
facts.hook: a sealed bag of chips puffs up during the flight

facts.fact: Swallowing or yawning opens the Eustachian tubes, which lets air into the middle ear and relieves the pressure people feel in their ears as a plane descends.
facts.hook: a little sibling cries during landing until someone hands them a drink

facts.fact: Motion sickness happens when the eyes and the balance organs in the inner ear send the brain conflicting signals about whether the body is moving.
facts.hook: reading a book in the back seat on a winding road leaves a kid nauseated

facts.fact: Looking at the horizon, a fixed distant point, can ease motion sickness because it helps the eyes agree with what the inner ear feels.
facts.hook: a queasy passenger on a ferry feels better after going on deck and watching the shoreline

facts.fact: Yellowstone became the first national park in the United States on March 1, 1872, when President Ulysses S. Grant signed it into law.
facts.hook: a park ranger's quiz question stumps a whole family at a campfire talk

facts.fact: Leave No Trace outdoor ethics are organized as seven principles, including 'dispose of waste properly' and 'leave what you find'.
facts.hook: a kid wants to take home a pretty rock from a national park and a sibling objects

facts.fact: Dermatologists advise reapplying sunscreen every two hours outdoors, and immediately after swimming or sweating.
facts.hook: a morning of sunscreen and an afternoon of swimming ends in a sunburn at the beach

facts.fact: A swimmer caught in a rip current can usually escape by swimming parallel to the beach, out of the narrow current, rather than straight against it.
facts.hook: a lifeguard's sign at the beach makes one kid ask what to do if the water pulls them out

facts.fact: Fire-safety guidance says to put out a campfire by drowning it with water, stirring the ashes, and drowning it again until everything is cool to the touch.
facts.hook: a family is ready to leave the campsite but the fire pit is still warm

facts.fact: In bear country, parks such as Yosemite count anything with a scent as 'food', so toothpaste, sunscreen and trash must go in the bear locker too.
facts.hook: a camper leaves toothpaste in the tent and a parent sends them back to the locker

facts.fact: The 'butterflies' people feel when nervous come from adrenaline, which speeds up the heart and pulls blood away from the stomach toward the muscles.
facts.hook: a fourteen-year-old cannot finish lunch on the day of a first movie date

facts.fact: Blushing happens when blood vessels in the face widen and let more blood flow near the skin.
facts.hook: someone turns red when their date laughs at their joke and wants to hide it

facts.fact: In his 1872 book on emotions, Charles Darwin called blushing 'the most peculiar and the most human of all expressions'.
facts.hook: a nervous teen jokes about their red face, and their date quotes a scientist

facts.fact: Open-ended questions, which cannot be answered with just yes or no, usually get longer answers and keep a conversation going.
facts.hook: a coffee shop conversation keeps dying after 'Do you like school?'

facts.fact: Teen safety guides advise telling a parent or trusted adult where you are going, who you will be with and when you will be home.
facts.hook: a teen heading to the bowling alley texts a parent the plan before leaving

facts.fact: Either person on a date can say no to holding hands, a hug or a kiss at any time, and a respectful partner accepts that answer without pressure.
facts.hook: at the end of a date one person pulls back from a hug and the other has to decide how to react

facts.fact: The PG-13 movie rating was introduced in the United States on July 1, 1984, as a step between PG and R.
facts.hook: two teens at a movie theater argue about which movie they are allowed to see

facts.fact: In the United States, a PG-13 rating warns parents that some material in a movie may be inappropriate for children under 13.
facts.hook: a younger sibling wants to tag along on a movie date and the rating settles it

facts.fact: A perfect game in ten-pin bowling scores 300 and takes 12 strikes in a row.
facts.hook: a date at the bowling alley brags about a 'perfect game' of 150

facts.fact: In bowling, a strike scores 10 points plus the pins knocked down with the next two balls.
facts.hook: two teens at the bowling alley cannot figure out why the screen shows a bigger score than they expected

facts.fact: When each person pays for their own share of a bill, it is often called 'going Dutch'.
facts.hook: an awkward moment at the coffee shop counter over who should pay

facts.fact: Active listening means giving someone full attention and then showing you heard them, for example by asking a follow-up question about what they said.
facts.hook: a teen realizes they have talked about themselves for the whole walk around the mall

facts.fact: Stage fright is the body's fight-or-flight response: adrenaline can cause a racing heart, a dry mouth, a shaky voice and trembling hands.
facts.hook: a singer backstage at the school concert cannot stop their hands shaking

facts.fact: Stage left and stage right are the performers' left and right as they stand facing the audience.
facts.hook: a choir member walks off the wrong side because the teacher said 'exit stage left'

facts.fact: Upstage is the back of the stage, farthest from the audience, and downstage is the front, nearest the audience.
facts.hook: a nervous performer steps 'upstage' and ends up behind everyone else

facts.fact: Performers often say 'break a leg' instead of 'good luck', because of an old theatre superstition that wishing good luck brings bad luck.
facts.hook: a younger sibling says 'good luck' in the dressing room and an older cast member gasps

facts.fact: The squeal of microphone feedback happens when sound from a loudspeaker goes back into the microphone, gets amplified again, and loops louder and louder.
facts.hook: a sound check at the school concert is ruined by a piercing whistle

facts.fact: To avoid feedback, microphones should not be pointed at the loudspeakers or held in front of them.
facts.hook: a soloist walks toward the front speaker and the microphone starts to howl

facts.fact: Orchestras tune to a concert A played by the oboe, because its pitch is steady and its penetrating sound is easy for everyone to hear.
facts.hook: a nervous violinist wonders why the whole orchestra waits for one oboe note

facts.fact: The standard tuning pitch for the A above middle C is 440 vibrations per second, an international standard known as A440.
facts.hook: a tuner app shows '440' and a kid wants to know why that number

facts.fact: In a 2000 study, psychologist Thomas Gilovich and colleagues found people greatly overestimate how much others notice their appearance or mistakes, which is called the spotlight effect.
facts.hook: a singer who missed one note is sure everyone heard it, but no friend noticed

facts.fact: A dress rehearsal is a full run-through shortly before the first performance, done as if it were the real show, usually in costume.
facts.hook: at the dress rehearsal, a costume turns out too tight to breathe in for singing

facts.fact: A curtain call is when performers return to the stage at the end of a show to be recognized by the audience, usually with a bow.
facts.hook: the performers forget to rehearse the ending bow and freeze on stage during the applause

facts.fact: The downbeat is the first beat of each bar, which a conductor shows with a downward stroke of the hand or baton.
facts.hook: a choir member who lost count in the song finds the place again by watching the conductor

facts.fact: The first call from a handheld cellular phone was made by Motorola engineer Martin Cooper on a New York street on April 3, 1973.
facts.hook: a kid at the phone store wonders how long people have had phones in their pockets

facts.fact: The phone Martin Cooper used for the first handheld cell phone call weighed about 1.1 kilograms (2.5 pounds).
facts.hook: a grandparent at the kitchen table laughs at how light the new phone is

facts.fact: Steve Jobs announced the first iPhone on January 9, 2007.
facts.hook: a parent realizes their child's first phone is newer than the phone they grew up without

facts.fact: Most mobile phones can call the emergency number 112 even when the phone is locked; in North America, a call to 112 is usually redirected to 911.
facts.hook: a friend's locked phone is the only one around when someone gets hurt

facts.fact: Two-factor authentication asks for a second proof, such as a code sent to your phone, so a stolen password alone is not enough to get into an account.
facts.hook: a kid gets a login code they never asked for and realizes someone has their password

facts.fact: Phishing is a scam in which someone pretends to be a trusted company or person to trick you into giving away passwords or other private information.
facts.hook: a text saying a game account will be deleted unless you 'verify your password' arrives on day one

facts.fact: The US standards agency NIST says length is the most important part of a password, so a long passphrase beats a short password full of symbols.
facts.hook: a new phone owner picks 'Dog!1' as a password and a friend challenges it

facts.fact: Blue-enriched light from phone screens can reduce or delay the body's release of melatonin, the hormone that makes you sleepy in the evening.
facts.hook: a kid who scrolls in bed every night keeps struggling to fall asleep

facts.fact: Phone batteries are lithium-ion, and as they chemically age they hold less charge, so battery life slowly gets shorter.
facts.hook: a hand-me-down phone dies by lunchtime every day

facts.fact: Streaming video uses far more mobile data than sending text messages, so watching videos away from Wi-Fi can use up a data plan quickly.
facts.hook: a monthly data plan runs out in a week of watching videos on the bus

facts.fact: Airplane mode turns off a phone's radio signals, including the cellular connection it uses for calls and texts.
facts.hook: a kid at a friend's house cannot figure out why no messages are coming through

facts.fact: Apps must ask permission to use a phone's camera, microphone or contacts, and you can take that permission away later in the phone's settings.
facts.hook: a flashlight app asks to see all your contacts and a new phone owner stops to think

facts.fact: Chocolate contains theobromine, which dogs break down very slowly, and dark or baking chocolate is far more dangerous to them than milk chocolate.
facts.hook: a new puppy gets into a bag of baking chocolate and the family calls the vet

facts.fact: Grapes and raisins can cause kidney damage in dogs, so they should never be given as treats.
facts.hook: a kid about to share trail mix with the dog at the park is stopped by a friend

facts.fact: Xylitol, a sweetener in some sugar-free gum and candy, makes a dog's body release insulin and can cause a dangerous drop in blood sugar.
facts.hook: sugar-free gum left in a backpack becomes an emergency at the vet clinic

facts.fact: Cats are obligate carnivores, which means they depend on nutrients found in animal flesh and cannot stay healthy on a vegetarian diet.
facts.hook: a vegetarian family wonders whether their new kitten can eat like they do

facts.fact: Cats cannot make enough of their own taurine, a nutrient found in meat, and a lack of it can cause heart disease and blindness.
facts.hook: a kid at the pet store wonders why cat food and dog food are not the same

facts.fact: Like humans, guinea pigs cannot make their own vitamin C, so they must get it from their food every day.
facts.hook: a new guinea pig gets sick on a diet of dry pellets and nothing fresh

facts.fact: A guinea pig's front teeth never stop growing, so it needs things to chew on to wear them down.
facts.hook: a guinea pig starts gnawing the bars of its cage and the owner learns why

facts.fact: A new fish tank needs weeks for bacteria to grow that turn toxic ammonia from fish waste into nitrite and then into less harmful nitrate.
facts.hook: goldfish added the same day the tank is set up start dying within a week

facts.fact: A pet microchip is about the size of a grain of rice and holds an ID number that a scanner reads to find the owner's contact details.
facts.hook: a shelter worker scans a lost dog and finds its family in minutes

facts.fact: A pet microchip has no GPS and cannot track where an animal is; it only gives its ID number when a scanner is held close.
facts.hook: a kid expects to see a missing cat on a phone map because it is microchipped

facts.fact: Cats purr when they are content, but they also purr when they are in pain or stressed, as a way to soothe themselves.
facts.hook: a purring cat that will not eat turns out to be sick at the vet clinic

facts.fact: True lilies are highly toxic to cats, so they are unsafe to keep in a home with a cat.
facts.hook: a bouquet of lilies arrives for a birthday in a house with a new kitten

facts.fact: In nearsightedness, light from distant objects focuses in front of the retina instead of on it, most often because the eyeball is slightly too long.
facts.hook: a student cannot read the board from the back row but reads a phone perfectly

facts.fact: Eyeglass prescriptions measure lens strength in diopters, with a minus sign for nearsightedness and a plus sign for farsightedness.
facts.hook: a kid reads '-2.00' on their prescription and worries it means their eyes got a negative score

facts.fact: In farsightedness, light focuses behind the retina, so near objects look blurry, and it is corrected with convex lenses.
facts.hook: a friend's glasses make a student's eyes look bigger while their own make them look smaller

facts.fact: Astigmatism happens when the cornea or lens is slightly egg-shaped, curving more in one direction than the other, which blurs vision at any distance.
facts.hook: an optometrist explains why letters look smeared both near and far

facts.fact: Glasses for astigmatism use cylindrical lenses, which bend light more in one direction than in the other.
facts.hook: a kid notices that turning their new lens sideways makes the world look stretched

facts.fact: Herman Snellen developed his eye chart of rows of shrinking letters in 1862.
facts.hook: a school nurse's eye chart turns out to be older than anyone's great-grandparents

facts.fact: 20/40 vision means you must stand 20 feet away to read letters that a person with normal eyesight can read from 40 feet.
facts.hook: a kid thinks 20/40 vision is better than 20/20 because the number is bigger

facts.fact: Countries that use metres write normal vision as 6/6 instead of 20/20; both describe the same eyesight.
facts.hook: a cousin from overseas says they have '6/6 vision' and a kid thinks something is wrong

facts.fact: The earliest eyeglasses were made in central Italy around 1290.
facts.hook: a kid at the eyeglasses store wonders how people read before glasses existed

facts.fact: Benjamin Franklin, who was nearsighted and also needed help seeing up close, is credited with inventing bifocals.
facts.hook: a grandparent's glasses with a line across each lens puzzle a kid getting their first pair

facts.fact: Studies show that nearsightedness is less common in people who spent more time outdoors during childhood.
facts.hook: a kid who spends all weekend indoors on screens hears the optometrist's advice

facts.fact: On eye prescriptions, OD means the right eye and OS means the left eye, from the Latin oculus dexter and oculus sinister.
facts.hook: a kid at the optometrist's office thinks OD and OS are codes for something scary

facts.fact: After about age 40, the lens of the eye loses flexibility and cannot focus up close as well, a condition called presbyopia that reading glasses correct.
facts.hook: a visiting grandparent holds the menu at arm's length at a local market cafe

facts.fact: Age-related hearing loss usually affects high-pitched sounds first, so voices can sound muffled even when they are loud enough.
facts.hook: a grandparent can hear a grandchild's voice but keeps missing the words

facts.fact: People with age-related hearing loss find it especially hard to follow speech when there is background noise.
facts.hook: a conversation that worked at home falls apart in a busy train station

facts.fact: Facing a person with hearing loss and speaking clearly helps them understand more than shouting does.
facts.hook: a kid who shouts from the next room learns to walk over and talk face to face

facts.fact: Age-related hearing loss is very common, affecting roughly one in three people by age 65.
facts.hook: a kid is surprised to learn how many classmates' grandparents use hearing aids

facts.fact: The body's sense of thirst weakens with age, so older people can become dehydrated without feeling thirsty.
facts.hook: on a hot day at the park, a grandparent says they are not thirsty, and a grandchild brings water anyway

facts.fact: The sense of smell naturally declines in old age, a change called presbyosmia.
facts.hook: a grandparent cannot smell the burning toast that fills the kitchen

facts.fact: In the United States, falls are the leading cause of injury death for adults aged 65 and older.
facts.hook: a family moves a loose rug out of the guest room before a grandparent arrives

facts.fact: A pill organizer has a compartment for each day of the week, so an empty compartment shows that day's dose has already been taken.
facts.hook: a grandparent cannot remember whether they took the morning pills until a grandchild checks the box

facts.fact: Older adults are at greater risk of hypothermia, a dangerous drop in body temperature, than younger adults.
facts.hook: a grandparent sits in a chilly room without complaining, and a grandchild turns up the heat

facts.fact: National Grandparents Day in the United States falls on the first Sunday after Labor Day and was proclaimed by President Jimmy Carter in 1978.
facts.hook: a grandparent's week-long visit happens to include a holiday nobody in the family knew about

facts.fact: StoryCorps is a project in which people record interviews with family members, and with permission the recordings are saved at the Library of Congress.
facts.hook: a grandchild records a grandparent's childhood stories on the last night of the visit

facts.fact: Philosopher Karl Popper argued, in a book first published in 1934, that an idea is scientific only if some possible observation could prove it wrong.
facts.hook: a science fair judge asks what result would show a student's idea was false

facts.fact: No number of white swans can prove that all swans are white, but seeing a single black swan proves that claim false.
facts.hook: a kid claims every cat hates water until a friend's cat jumps into the bath

facts.fact: The word hypothesis comes from ancient Greek and literally means 'putting or placing under'.
facts.hook: a student looks up the word for a science fair board and finds a surprise

facts.fact: In science, a theory is not a guess; it is an explanation that has been repeatedly tested and supported, while a hypothesis is an idea still being tested.
facts.hook: a sibling says evolution is 'just a theory' and a science-centre guide responds

facts.fact: A null hypothesis is the statement that there is no relationship between the things being studied, which an experiment then tries to reject.
facts.hook: two friends testing whether music helps plants grow must say what 'no effect' would look like

facts.fact: The independent variable is the one thing an experimenter changes on purpose to see what happens.
facts.hook: a garage experiment changes both the paper and the wing shape and can't tell which mattered

facts.fact: A control group is treated exactly like the test group except for the one thing being tested, so any difference can be traced to that change.
facts.hook: a plant-fertilizer project has no untreated plants to compare against

facts.fact: In a fair test, everything except the variable being tested is kept the same, such as the amount, the temperature and the timing.
facts.hook: one paper airplane is thrown indoors and the other outside in the wind

facts.fact: In 1668 Francesco Redi put meat in jars; maggots grew in open jars, but not in jars covered with gauze that kept flies off the meat.
facts.hook: a kid at home insists rotting fruit makes fruit flies all by itself

facts.fact: Louis Pasteur boiled broth in flasks with long S-shaped necks; the broth stayed free of microbes because dust and germs got trapped in the bend of the neck.
facts.hook: a science fair student wonders why a jar of soup went bad while a sealed one did not

facts.fact: Repeating an experiment several times helps show whether a result is real or just happened by chance.
facts.hook: a toy car wins one race down the ramp and its owner declares it the fastest forever

facts.fact: Hypotheses are often written as 'If ..., then ...' statements, which name the change being made and the result that is predicted.
facts.hook: a science fair poster says 'plants like music' and a teacher asks how that could be tested
